title: Obligations III — sale and warranty (class 2 Dec)

1.title: Warranty in general
1.text:
Lesson for the class of 2 December 2026 (Obligations; sale, warranty). Assessment II on 13 January 2027 is an exegesis of a Digest fragment on the law of obligations, so a warranty fragment is a realistic exam text. Doctrine: Benke/Meissel, *Roman Law of Obligations* (RLO), ch. VI, pp. 146–176; property law from Benke/Meissel, *Roman Law of Property* (RLP). The class also uses RLO pp. 160–161 (CAVEAT EMPTOR, sales talk, the edict of the curule aediles).

### What warranty is
A sale (EMPTIO VENDITIO) obliges the buyer to pay the price and the seller to deliver the goods. But the obligation does not simply end with delivery and payment: a flaw in the performance may come to light later. **Warranty** is the seller's liability for such defects (RLO p. 146). Two kinds:
- **defect of title**: a third person takes the thing away from the buyer with an action IN REM (Example 54: Niketas, the civil-law owner, wins a REI VINDICATIO against the buyer Melitta);
- **defect of quality**: the thing itself is faulty (Example 55: a cow already diseased at delivery has to be put down).

### Three features (RLO pp. 147–148)
1. **Liability regardless of fault.** The seller answers for the defect in principle whether or not he caused it or knew of it. DOLUS (malicious intent) makes his liability stricter.
2. **The defect must exist at delivery.** Its cause is enough: an animal already infected counts even if the illness breaks out later. Defects arising **after delivery** give no warranty.
3. **Warranty can be restricted or excluded by agreement** (it is dispositive), but never for DOLUS MALUS: excluding liability for malice is against BONA FIDES (Pomponius D 19.1.6.9, Case 101).

### Link to risk (ch. V)
What happens between conclusion and delivery is not warranty but risk or non-performance. Once the sale is **perfected** (price fixed, object individually specified, no suspensive condition or term), the buyer bears the risk of accidental loss or deterioration: PERICULUM EST EMPTORIS (RLO pp. 127–128). So a defect that arises **by accident after perfection** is the buyer's risk; one caused by the **seller's fault** before delivery is non-performance (pp. 147, 159). Paulus D 21.2.11 pr: later grounds of eviction arising after the sale do not concern the seller (p. 147 fn 3).

terms.def: The seller's liability, in principle regardless of fault, for defects of title or quality that exist at delivery and come to light afterwards (RLO pp. 146–147).
From perfection of the sale the buyer bears the risk of accidental loss or deterioration of the goods, both non-performance and payment risk (RLO pp. 127–128).
A sale whose price is fixed, whose object is individually specified, and whose effects no longer depend on a suspensive condition or term (RLO p. 127).

cards.q: What is warranty in the Roman law of sale?
cards.a:
The seller's liability for defects of the goods that exist at delivery and appear afterwards.
• Two kinds: defects of title and defects of quality
• In principle regardless of the seller's fault (RLO pp. 146–147)

cards.q: Which two kinds of defect does Roman warranty cover? Give an example of each.
cards.a:
Defects of title and defects of quality.
• Title: the civil-law owner wins a REI VINDICATIO against the buyer (Example 54)
• Quality: a cow already diseased at delivery must be put down (Example 55)

cards.q: Does the seller's warranty depend on his fault?
cards.a:
No: he answers for the defect in principle whether or not he caused it or knew of it.
• DOLUS (malicious intent) makes his liability stricter (RLO p. 147)

cards.q: At what point must a defect exist to give warranty claims?
cards.a:
At delivery; it is enough that its cause exists then (e.g. an animal already infected).
• Arose by accident after perfection but before delivery → risk (PERICULUM EST EMPTORIS)
• Caused by the seller's fault before delivery → non-performance
• Arose after delivery → no warranty

cards.q: Can the parties exclude the seller's warranty?
cards.a:
Yes, warranty is dispositive, but never for DOLUS MALUS.
• Excluding liability for malice is against BONA FIDES (Pomponius D 19.1.6.9, Case 101)
• So a seller who knowingly concealed a defect is liable despite a total waiver

cards.q: What does PERICULUM EST EMPTORIS mean, and when does it apply?
cards.a:
From perfection of the sale the buyer bears the risk of accidental loss or deterioration.
• He gets no goods and no damages, yet must pay the price
• Perfection: price fixed, object specified, no suspensive condition or term (RLO pp. 127–128)

2.title: Property law you need for warranty
2.text:
Warranty of title is an **obligations** problem caused by a **property** problem. Keep the two levels apart (RLO pp. 148–149): whether the sale is valid and what the parties owe is the law of obligations; whether a valid TRADITIO took place and whether the buyer became owner is property law.

### Why a non-owner can sell
A sale only creates claims. The seller's ownership has no bearing on the validity of the sale, so one can validly sell another person's thing (Ulpian D 18.1.28, Case 95/2). Exceptions: buying one's own thing is impossible; a sale of a stolen thing (RES FURTIVA) is not valid if both parties know it is stolen (RLO p. 149).

### Why the buyer does not become owner
**TRADITIO** (informal delivery) passes ownership only if three requirements are met: an authorised transferor (owner or someone with power of disposal), transfer of possession, and a IUSTA CAUSA TRADITIONIS such as a sale (RLP pp. 84–85). **NEMO PLUS IURIS TRANSFERRE POTEST QUAM IPSE HABET** (Ulpian D 41.1.20 pr): nobody can transfer more rights than he has. So a buyer from a non-owner gets **possession, not ownership** (RLP p. 101).

### MANCIPATIO and AUCTORITAS
**MANCIPATIO** is the formal civil-law conveyance with scales and five witnesses, for RES MANCIPI (Italian land, slaves, draught and pack animals). A non-owner cannot convey by it either (RLP pp. 82–83). A mere TRADITIO of a RES MANCIPI gives only bonitarian ownership (RLP p. 85). In a mancipation sale the seller must assist the buyer in court against a third party's claim: AUCTORITATEM PRAESTARE (RLO p. 152).

### Eviction = a third party wins IN REM
The true owner sues the buyer with the **REI VINDICATIO**: the quirite owner's action against any possessor (UBI REM MEAM INVENIO, IBI VINDICO, RLP p. 160). The formula has a CLAUSULA ARBITRARIA: the defendant may return the thing; otherwise he is condemned in money (OMNIS CONDEMNATIO PECUNIARIA EST, RLP pp. 156–158). A usucapient or bonitarian owner sues with the **ACTIO PUBLICIANA**; the true owner defeats it with the EXCEPTIO IUSTI DOMINII (RLP pp. 168–170).

### USUCAPIO cures the defect
The good-faith buyer can become owner by **USUCAPIO**: RES HABILIS (not stolen: LEX ATINIA), TITULUS (the sale), BONA FIDES, POSSESSIO, TEMPUS of one year for movables and two for land (RLP pp. 102–108). This is why Roman law waits for eviction (RLO p. 151).

terms.term: NEMO PLUS IURIS TRANSFERRE POTEST QUAM IPSE HABET
terms.def: Nobody can transfer more rights than he himself has (Ulpian D 41.1.20 pr); a buyer from a non-owner gets possession, not ownership (RLP pp. 77, 101; RLO p. 150).
The quirite owner's action IN REM against any possessor; with CLAUSULA ARBITRARIA, otherwise condemnation in money (RLP pp. 156–160).
Original acquisition of ownership by qualified possession over one year (movables) or two years (land); requirements RES HABILIS, TITULUS, BONA FIDES, POSSESSIO, TEMPUS (RLP pp. 99–108).
Formal civil-law conveyance of RES MANCIPI with scales, scale-holder and five witnesses; abstract but derivative (RLP pp. 82–83).

cards.q: Can a person validly sell a thing he does not own?
cards.a:
Yes: the sale only creates claims, so the seller's ownership does not affect its validity (Ulpian D 18.1.28).
• Exceptions: buying one's own thing; selling a RES FURTIVA when both know it is stolen

cards.q: Why does a buyer who receives a thing from a non-owner by TRADITIO not become owner?
cards.a:
Because of NEMO PLUS IURIS TRANSFERRE POTEST QUAM IPSE HABET: the seller cannot transfer a right he lacks.
• The buyer gets possession, not ownership
• TRADITIO needs an authorised transferor, transfer of possession and a IUSTA CAUSA

cards.q: What is eviction in property-law terms?
cards.a:
A third party successfully enforces a right IN REM in the thing against the buyer.
• Typically a REI VINDICATIO or ACTIO PUBLICIANA
• Also enforcing a limited real right, e.g. VINDICATIO PIGNORIS (RLO pp. 150–151)

cards.q: What are the five requirements of USUCAPIO, and how long is the period?
cards.a:
RES HABILIS, TITULUS, BONA FIDES, POSSESSIO, TEMPUS.
• One year for movables, two years for land
• Stolen things are not RES HABILIS (LEX ATINIA)

cards.q: Why does USUCAPIO matter for warranty of title?
cards.a:
It cures the defect: the good-faith buyer becomes owner when the period ends.
• So he may never suffer from the failed transfer of ownership
• This justifies waiting for eviction (RLO p. 151)

cards.q: What do the CLAUSULA ARBITRARIA and OMNIS CONDEMNATIO PECUNIARIA EST mean in the REI VINDICATIO?
cards.a:
The judge cannot order return of the thing; he invites the defendant to restore it, otherwise condemns him to pay its value.
• Eviction occurs either way: on return or on condemnation (RLO p. 151)

3.title: Defects of title: the principle of eviction and the buyer's claims
3.text:
### What the seller owes
The Roman seller must deliver and guarantee **peaceable possession**: the buyer must be able to use, take fruits and possess, UTI FRUI HABERE LICERE (LICERE HABERE, Julian D 21.2.8, Case 100). He need **not** make the buyer owner (RLO p. 150).

### Principle of eviction (RLO pp. 150–152)
The mere fact that the buyer did not become owner gives him no claim. Warranty of title starts only with **eviction**. It occurs when the buyer, sued IN REM, (1) surrenders the thing under the CLAUSULA ARBITRARIA, (2) is condemned to pay its value, or (3) has lost possession, sues the owner IN REM himself and loses (Pomponius D 21.2.16.1, Case 103). Chain of sales: each buyer claims from his own seller, the last buyer first (Marcellus D 21.2.61, Case 105). Reason: while the buyer possesses peaceably, performance is not defective, and USUCAPIO may cure the defect.

### Claims upon eviction (RLO pp. 152–155)
- **Mancipation sale → ACTIO AUCTORITATIS** for double the price (DUPLUM). The buyer must call on the seller to assist in the lawsuit; if he does not, the seller may raise the defences he could have used against the third party (Example 56: the EXCEPTIO REI VENDITAE ET TRADITAE).
- **STIPULATIO DUPLAE**: the seller promises REM EMPTAM ET TRADITAM NON EVICTAM ESSE, usually for double the price; on eviction the buyer sues with a **CONDICTIO**. If no amount was agreed, the SIMPLUM (the price) is owed (Javolenus D 21.2.60, Case 96). For market slaves, valuables and provincial land the seller apparently had to give it (enforceable by ACTIO EMPTI).
- **ACTIO EMPTI**: the evicted buyer gets his **expectation interest**: the value of the thing plus every advantage lost through eviction. Without a stipulation he gets at least what a stipulation would have given (Paul Sent 2.17.2). Even with a STIPULATIO DUPLAE he may sue on the sale if his interest is higher (Example 57).

### Exceptions: claims without eviction (RLO pp. 155–157)
1. The seller **knew** he could not dispose of the thing → ACTIO EMPTI for the interest in becoming owner, based on BONA FIDES (Africanus D 19.1.30.1, Case 102).
2. The seller **stipulated to procure ownership** → action on the stipulation (Ulpian D 18.1.25.1, Case 95/1).
3. Possession undisturbed **EX ALIA CAUSA**: the buyer becomes the owner's heir (Paulus D 21.2.9, Case 107) or buys the thing from the owner (Pomponius D 21.2.29 pr, Case 106) → ACTIO EMPTI, but **no** action on the STIPULATIO DUPLAE, since technically there was no eviction.

terms.def: Roman warranty of title applies only once a third party has evicted the buyer, not merely because he did not become owner (RLO pp. 150–152).
The buyer's peaceable possession (use, fruits, possession) that the seller must procure; briefly LICERE HABERE (RLO p. 150).
The seller's stipulation that the sold and delivered thing will not be evicted, usually for double the price; enforced by CONDICTIO (RLO p. 153).
The buyer's action for double the price after eviction in a mancipation sale (RLO p. 152).
Undisturbed possession resting on another legal ground (succession to the owner), not on the seller's performance (RLO p. 156).

cards.q: What is the principle of eviction?
cards.a:
Warranty of title claims generally depend on eviction, not on the mere lack of ownership.
• Counter-concept: principle of procuring ownership (modern Austrian law)
• Reason: peaceable possession = no defective performance; USUCAPIO may cure the defect

cards.q: When has a buyer been evicted in the Roman sense?
cards.a:
When a third party has successfully enforced a right IN REM against him.
• He surrenders the thing under the CLAUSULA ARBITRARIA, or
• he is condemned to pay its value, or
• he lost possession, sued IN REM himself and lost (Pomponius D 21.2.16.1)

cards.q: Which remedy does the buyer have upon eviction in a (1) mancipation sale, (2) sale with a stipulation, (3) plain EMPTIO VENDITIO?
cards.a: (1) ACTIO AUCTORITATIS; (2) action on the stipulation (CONDICTIO); (3) ACTIO EMPTI (RLO p. 152).

cards.q: What is the ACTIO AUCTORITATIS, and what must the buyer do to keep it intact?
cards.a:
The buyer's action for DUPLUM of the price after eviction in a mancipation sale.
• He must call on the seller to assist (AUCTORITATEM PRAESTARE) in the lawsuit
• Otherwise the seller may raise the defences he could have raised against the third party

cards.q: What does the seller promise in a STIPULATIO DUPLAE, and how is it enforced?
cards.a:
That the sold and delivered thing will not be evicted (REM EMPTAM ET TRADITAM NON EVICTAM ESSE), usually for double the price.
• Enforced by CONDICTIO
• No amount agreed → SIMPLUM, i.e. the price (D 21.2.60)

cards.q: What can the evicted buyer claim with the ACTIO EMPTI?
cards.a:
His expectation interest: the value of the thing plus every advantage lost through eviction.
• E.g. an inheritance entered by the slave on the buyer's order; the child of a female slave (Julian D 21.2.8)
• At least what a STIPULATIO DUPLAE would have given (Paul Sent 2.17.2)

cards.q: Chain sale (Example 57): vase worth 100 sold to Omphale for 100 with STIPULATIO DUPLAE; she resells to Quinta for 120, also with DUPLUM; the owner Eros evicts Quinta. What can each claim?
cards.a:
Quinta: 240 from Omphale on the stipulation.
• Omphale: 200 from Pomona on the stipulation, or 240 (her interest) with the ACTIO EMPTI → the ACTIO EMPTI is better

cards.q: In which three situations can the buyer claim for a defect of title without eviction?
cards.a:
1) The seller knew he could not dispose → ACTIO EMPTI (D 19.1.30.1).
• 2) The seller stipulated to procure ownership → action on the stipulation (D 18.1.25.1)
• 3) Possession undisturbed EX ALIA CAUSA → ACTIO EMPTI (D 21.2.29 pr; D 21.2.9)

cards.q: The buyer of another's thing later buys it from the true owner (or becomes the owner's heir). Can he sue his seller?
cards.a:
Yes, with the ACTIO EMPTI, derived from BONA FIDES: possession undisturbed EX ALIA CAUSA.
• Not on the STIPULATIO DUPLAE: technically no eviction, so its condition is not met (Pomponius D 21.2.29 pr; Paulus D 21.2.9)

4.title: Defects of quality I: concept, CAVEAT EMPTOR and the aediles' edict
4.text:
### What a defect of quality is (RLO pp. 158–159)
A defect inherent in the thing that impairs its **ordinary** or its **expressly agreed** use.
- **Ordinary use**: without other agreement the thing must have the qualities normally expected of its kind. Timber must not be rotten (D 19.1.13 pr), amphorae must not leak (D 19.1.6.4).
- **Agreed use**: the seller's oral assurances and promises (**DICTA ET PROMISSA**) set the standard: a vessel of a promised capacity (D 19.1.6.4), a female slave sold as a virgin (D 19.1.11.5), a slave called an *excellent* cook rather than just a cook (D 21.1.18.1). The parties can also agree on features that would otherwise be defects: second-hand clothes are worn (D 18.1.45). So the test is always the **ID QUOD ACTUM EST**, what the parties agreed.
- **Duty of disclosure**: under BONA FIDES the seller must tell the buyer of defects; DOLUS also covers slyly hiding something (Florentinus D 18.1.43.2). Example 58: Leda conceals that Bruno's mortal enemy owns the neighbouring estate → warranty claims.

### No warranty: CAVEAT EMPTOR and sales talk (RLO p. 160)
- **Apparent defects** give no claims; a buyer who does not inspect carefully bears the consequences: **CAVEAT EMPTOR**, "let the buyer beware". This only concerns visible qualities: that a slave is good-looking the buyer must check himself; that he has learnt a trade the seller answers for (Florentinus D 18.1.43 pr, Case 118).
- **Mere praise** of one's goods creates no warranty where it is clear the seller did not mean to bind himself (Ulpian D 21.1.19 pr, Case 132).

### The edict of the curule aediles (RLO pp. 160–162)
The curule aediles supervised the markets and, as magistrates, had the IUS EDICENDI. Their edict on market sales of **slaves** and of **IUMENTA** (draught and pack animals) and **PECORA** (herd animals) required the seller to declare any **MORBUS** (any but very slight illness) and **VITIA**: being a FUGITIVUS (runaway) or ERRO (loiterer), and noxal liability. The declaration informs the buyer, so price and goods stay equivalent, and works as a **guarantee**: the seller is liable for an undisclosed defect **whether or not he knew of it**.

### Aedilician remedies (RLO pp. 162–164)
- **ACTIO REDHIBITORIA** (within **six months**): rescission EX TUNC with mutual restitution; consequential losses may be considered; return of the thing is in principle required, but **MORTUUS REDHIBETUR** (Ulpian D 21.1.31.11, Case 128).
- **ACTIO QUANTI MINORIS** (within **twelve months**): price reduction by what the buyer would have paid less had he known.

terms.def: 'Let the buyer beware': apparent defects give no warranty claims; the buyer must inspect visible qualities himself (RLO p. 160).
The seller's oral assurances and promises about the goods; they define the agreed use and make him liable even without fault (RLO pp. 158, 167).
What the parties actually agreed; it decides whether the thing is defective (RLO p. 159).
Aedilician action to set aside the sale, with mutual restitution; six months (RLO pp. 162–163).
Aedilician action for price reduction by what the buyer would have paid less; twelve months (RLO p. 162).
Illness / fault of a slave or animal that the aediles' edict required the seller to declare; VITIA listed: FUGITIVUS, ERRO, noxal liability (RLO p. 161).

cards.q: What is a defect of quality?
cards.a:
A defect inherent in the thing sold that impairs its ordinary or its expressly agreed use (RLO p. 158).
• Ordinary: qualities normally expected of the kind
• Agreed: qualities the seller promised (DICTA ET PROMISSA)

cards.q: Why is the ID QUOD ACTUM EST decisive for quality defects?
cards.a:
Because the parties can raise or lower the standard by agreement.
• Raise: promised capacity, 'excellent cook'
• Lower: clothes sold as second-hand may be worn (D 18.1.45)

cards.q: What does CAVEAT EMPTOR mean in Roman law, and what are its limits?
cards.a:
'Let the buyer beware': apparent defects give no warranty claims (Florentinus D 18.1.43 pr).
• Only visible qualities: 'good-looking' the buyer checks himself
• 'Has learnt a trade' the seller answers for

cards.q: Does mere sales talk make the seller liable?
cards.a:
No, as far as it is clear that he did not mean to bind himself legally (Ulpian D 21.1.19 pr, Case 132).
• With blatant advertising the lack of intention is obvious (RLO p. 160)

cards.q: Who were the curule aediles, and which sales did their edict cover?
cards.a:
Roman magistrates for market supervision and jurisdiction, with the IUS EDICENDI.
• Market sales of slaves and of draught/pack animals (IUMENTA) and herd animals (PECORA)
• Other animals were not covered

cards.q: What did a slave-seller have to declare under the aediles' edict?
cards.a:
Any MORBUS and the listed VITIA: FUGITIVUS, ERRO, noxal liability.
• Not very slight illnesses (small fever); missing tongue yes, missing tooth no
• Gambling, drinking, lying etc. are outside the edict

cards.q: ACTIO REDHIBITORIA vs ACTIO QUANTI MINORIS: aim and time limit?
cards.a:
REDHIBITORIA: rescission EX TUNC with mutual restitution, within six months.
• QUANTI MINORIS: price reduction by what the buyer would have paid less, within twelve months
• Both regardless of the seller's knowledge

5.title: Defects of quality II: ACTIO EMPTI, consequential loss and guarantees
5.text:
### ACTIO EMPTI for everything outside the edict (RLO pp. 164–165)
Goods other than slaves and the listed animals are outside the aediles' jurisdiction, so the buyer uses the **ACTIO EMPTI**. Through BONA FIDES the aedilician rules became the standard here too: the ACTIO EMPTI can give **price reduction** (Ulpian/Julian D 19.1.13 pr, Case 116; D 19.1.13.1, Case 115) and **rescission with restitution** (Ulpian D 19.1.11.3, Case 121). Ulpian D 19.1.11.5 (slave falsely presented as a virgin): no REDHIBITIO, but rescission through the ACTIO EMPTI.

### Two kinds of loss (RLO pp. 165–166)
- **Loss caused by the defect**: the goods are worth less. Example 59: timber bought for 1,000 is only firewood worth 150 → 850.
- **Consequential loss**: the defect damages the buyer's other assets. Example 60: the bunk bed made of that timber collapses and crushes a desk worth 4,000.

Price reduction and rescission only restore the **equivalence** of goods and price. They do not cover consequential loss. That is available with the ACTIO EMPTI only if the seller **breached BONA FIDES**, which is fault-based: above all when he **knew** of the defect and did not disclose it (dolose conduct), or when his **DICTA ET PROMISSA** proved false. In the second case his knowledge does not matter: by virtue of the guarantee he is liable without fault (RLO pp. 166–167).

### The key rule (Julian)
Unaware seller → only what the buyer would have paid less. Knowing seller → all losses from the purchase (D 19.1.13 pr; Marcian D 18.1.45, Case 117). For the slave who is a **FUGITIVUS**, an unaware seller still owes a price reduction, because the edict made running away a defect; for a slave who is a **FUR** (thief), an unaware seller is not liable at all, since theft was not among the declarable defects (D 19.1.13.1, RLO p. 168).

### Guarantees (RLO pp. 168–170)
The fault principle yields to (implied) guarantees. Pomponius D 19.1.6.4 (Case 114): a seller who assured a vessel's capacity or soundness is liable if it falls short, and for wine that leaked. Without an assurance Pomponius reports a view requiring DOLUS MALUS, then, citing Labeo, the probably prevailing view: whoever sells defective vessels must answer for their soundness in any event. Paulus D 19.1.21.2 (Case 122): a table sold as thuja wood that is not → buyer's interest in not having been deceived, even if the seller did not know. Another reading inserts a NON: no valid sale. A quality stipulation gives ID QUOD INTEREST, not the double (p. 164 fn 58).

terms.def: The loss that the goods themselves are worth less because of the defect; covered by price reduction or rescission (RLO pp. 165–166).
Damage the defect causes to the buyer's other assets; recoverable with the ACTIO EMPTI only on breach of BONA FIDES or a guarantee (RLO p. 166).
The buyer's action on the sale, a BONAE FIDEI IUDICIUM; covers eviction, quality defects outside the edict, and consequential loss where the seller breached good faith (RLO pp. 154, 164–167).

cards.q: Which action does the buyer use for quality defects in goods outside the aediles' edict?
cards.a:
The ACTIO EMPTI.
• By analogy (via BONA FIDES) it gives price reduction or rescission with restitution (RLO pp. 164–165)

cards.q: Loss caused by a defect vs consequential loss: what is the difference? Give the book's examples.
cards.a:
Loss caused by the defect: the goods are worth less (timber for 1,000 is firewood worth 150 → 850).
• Consequential loss: harm to other assets (bunk bed from that timber collapses and crushes a desk worth 4,000)

cards.q: When can the buyer recover consequential loss under Roman law?
cards.a:
With the ACTIO EMPTI if the seller breached BONA FIDES.
• Above all: he knew of the defect and concealed it
• Or his DICTA ET PROMISSA proved false (then even without fault)

cards.q: Julian (D 19.1.13 pr): what does an unaware seller owe, and what a seller who knew of the defect?
cards.a:
Unaware: only what the buyer would have paid less.
• Knowing: all losses resulting from the purchase (e.g. the collapsed building)

cards.q: Julian (D 19.1.13.1): why is the unaware seller of a runaway slave liable, but not the unaware seller of a thief?
cards.a:
Being a FUGITIVUS had to be declared under the aediles' edict, so it was a quality defect even without knowledge → price reduction.
• Being a FUR was not declarable → defect only if the seller knew or assured the opposite

cards.q: Ulpian D 19.1.11.5: a seller lets the buyer believe a female slave is a virgin; she is not. Which remedy?
cards.a:
No ACTIO REDHIBITORIA, but rescission with the ACTIO EMPTI (restitution of both performances).
• Presumably because lack of virginity is no MORBUS or VITIUM within the edict
• Keeping her → presumably price reduction

cards.q: Pomponius D 19.1.6.4: a vessel sold without assurance leaks. Which views does he report?
cards.a:
One view: liable for the buyer's losses only with DOLUS MALUS.
• Labeo (probably prevailing): whoever sells defective vessels answers for their soundness in any event
• Supported by Sabinus' ruling on rented-out barrels

cards.q: Paulus D 19.1.21.2: a table is sold as thuja wood but is not. What does Paulus decide, and what is the textual problem?
cards.a:
Buyer gets his interest in not having been deceived, even if the seller did not know (presumed guarantee).
• Alternative reading EMPTIONEM <NON> ESSE: no valid sale (error as to quality); the interest would then be the reliance interest

6.title: Decision table: defect of title vs defect of quality
6.text:
Use this table to answer the three questions of the INTERPRETATIVE PART: which remedy, against whom, for what? The plaintiff is always the buyer (or the last buyer in a chain); the defendant is always **his own seller**. The third party who evicts is not a party to the warranty claim.

### Defect of title (RLO pp. 150–157)

| Situation | Remedy | For what |
|---|---|---|
| Eviction after a mancipation sale | ACTIO AUCTORITATIS | DUPLUM of the price; buyer must have called the seller in |
| Eviction, STIPULATIO DUPLAE given | CONDICTIO on the stipulation | double the price (other multiple if agreed; SIMPLUM if no amount) |
| Eviction, plain EMPTIO VENDITIO | ACTIO EMPTI | expectation interest: value + lost advantages; at least what a stipulation would give |
| Seller must give the stipulation (market slave, valuables, provincial land) but refuses | ACTIO EMPTI | the giving of the stipulation |
| No eviction, seller **knew** he could not dispose | ACTIO EMPTI | interest in having become owner |
| No eviction, ownership **stipulated** | action on the stipulation | the promised sum |
| Possession undisturbed **EX ALIA CAUSA** | ACTIO EMPTI (not the stipulation) | interest, e.g. what he paid the owner |
| Buyer has peaceable possession, nothing more | none yet | wait: eviction or USUCAPIO |

### Defect of quality (RLO pp. 158–170)

| Situation | Remedy | For what |
|---|---|---|
| Apparent defect, mere sales talk | none (CAVEAT EMPTOR) | — |
| Market slave or IUMENTA/PECORA, undisclosed MORBUS/VITIUM | ACTIO REDHIBITORIA (6 months) or ACTIO QUANTI MINORIS (12 months) | rescission + restitution / price reduction; knowledge irrelevant |
| Other goods, seller **unaware** | ACTIO EMPTI | price reduction or rescission (loss caused by the defect only) |
| Seller **knew** and concealed (DOLUS) | ACTIO EMPTI | full interest incl. consequential loss |
| False DICTA ET PROMISSA / guarantee (vessels, thuja table) | ACTIO EMPTI | full interest, even without fault |
| Quality stipulation | action on the stipulation | ID QUOD INTEREST |

### Not warranty at all
- Defect arose **by accident after perfection** → risk: PERICULUM EST EMPTORIS (pp. 127–128, 159).
- Defect arose **by the seller's fault before delivery** → non-performance (p. 159).
- Defect arose **after delivery** → no claim.
- Exclusion clause → valid, except against DOLUS MALUS (D 19.1.6.9).

cards.q: Against whom does the evicted buyer bring his warranty claim, and against whom does the true owner sue?
cards.a:
Warranty: the buyer against his own seller (IN PERSONAM).
• The true owner sues the buyer IN REM (REI VINDICATIO); that lawsuit is the eviction

cards.q: Market sale of a slave with an undisclosed illness vs sale of rotten timber by an unaware seller: which remedies?
cards.a:
Slave: ACTIO REDHIBITORIA (6 months) or ACTIO QUANTI MINORIS (12 months), regardless of knowledge.
• Timber: ACTIO EMPTI for price reduction or rescission, not consequential loss

7.title: Mini exegesis 1: D 21.2.8 (Julian; evicted slave), Case 100
7.text:
Benke/Meissel cite this fragment for three points (RLO pp. 150 fn 9, 154 fn 24, 26, 27). The facts below are built from those references; **read the full text in Watson before class** and adjust the facts to how Julian actually sets them out.

### BASIC PART
1. **Facts**: A sells a slave to B and delivers him. A was not the owner. The owner C sues B and takes the slave away. Variants used by the book: (a) before the eviction the slave had entered on an inheritance on B's order; (b) the slave was a woman who had a child (PARTUS ANCILLAE).
2. **Legal question**: What can B claim from A after the eviction? Does the claim include the inheritance and the child?
3. **Decision**: JULIAN. B can claim his interest that the slave had been A's, i.e. his interest in peaceable possession (LICERE HABERE). That interest includes the inheritance and the child, which shares the legal fate of its mother.

### INTERPRETATIVE PART
4. **Institution**: warranty of title in EMPTIO VENDITIO. The seller owes UTI FRUI HABERE LICERE, not ownership (p. 150). Property backdrop: NEMO PLUS IURIS, so B received only possession; C as owner vindicated.
5. **Claims**: C v B: return of the slave as owner (succeeds = eviction). B v A: compensation for the failed peaceable possession.
6. **Remedies**: C v B: REI VINDICATIO (surrender under the CLAUSULA ARBITRARIA or condemnation in money, p. 151). B v A: ACTIO EMPTI for expectation interest (p. 154). If a STIPULATIO DUPLAE was given: CONDICTIO for double the price; B may choose the ACTIO EMPTI when his interest is higher (p. 155). If the slave was bought at the market, A apparently had to give such a stipulation (Ulpian D 21.2.37.1, p. 154).

### DOGMATIC EXPLANATION
7. **Similar cases**: Example 57 (chain sale, 240 v 200); Pomponius D 21.2.29 pr (no eviction but possession EX ALIA CAUSA → ACTIO EMPTI); Africanus D 19.1.30.1 (knowing seller liable even before eviction).
8. **Controversies**: none reported by the book for this fragment.
9. **Dogmatic**: under the principle of eviction B had no claim until C won; from then the ACTIO EMPTI, a BONAE FIDEI IUDICIUM, measures his whole interest, not just the price. So everything B lost along with the slave is compensated. B's interest is protected; A bears the loss although he may not have known that the slave was not his: warranty is liability regardless of fault.

terms.def: Short form of the buyer's interest in peaceable possession; Julian D 21.2.8 (RLO p. 150 fn 9).
The child of a female slave; it shares her legal fate, so an evicted buyer is compensated for it as well (RLO p. 154).

cards.q: Julian D 21.2.8: a buyer is evicted from a slave. What can he claim with the ACTIO EMPTI?
cards.a:
His interest that the slave had been the seller's (LICERE HABERE): value plus every advantage lost.
• Incl. an inheritance the slave entered on the buyer's order
• Incl. the child of a female slave (PARTUS ANCILLAE)

cards.q: In an exegesis of an eviction fragment, which property-law steps explain why the buyer was evicted?
cards.a:
Seller not owner → NEMO PLUS IURIS → buyer got possession only.
• Owner sues with REI VINDICATIO (or ACTIO PUBLICIANA)
• Buyer surrenders or is condemned = eviction; USUCAPIO had not yet cured the defect

cards.q: Why is the evicted buyer often better off with the ACTIO EMPTI than with a STIPULATIO DUPLAE?
cards.a:
The stipulation gives a fixed double of the price; the ACTIO EMPTI gives his full interest, which may be higher.
• He may sue on the sale despite the stipulation (Javolenus D 21.2.60)

8.title: Mini exegesis 2: D 19.1.13 pr (Ulpian citing Julian; sick animal, faulty timber), Case 116
8.text:
Facts and decision as summarised in RLO p. 167.

### BASIC PART
1. **Facts**: Basic case: A sells B an animal that is sick; after delivery it infects B's other animals. Variant: A sells B building timber that is defective; the building B puts up with it collapses.
2. **Legal question**: What can B claim from A in each case, and does it depend on whether A knew of the defect?
3. **Decision**: ULPIAN reports JULIAN's opinion and follows it. If A did not know: he is liable only for what B would have paid less had he known. If A sold knowingly: he is liable for all losses resulting from the purchase: in the timber case the value of the collapsed building, in the animal case B's interest in having bought a healthy animal.

### INTERPRETATIVE PART
4. **Institution**: warranty for defects of quality in EMPTIO VENDITIO. Both defects existed at delivery (the cause is enough, p. 159) and impair ordinary use: timber must not be faulty (p. 158).
5. **Claims**: B v A: reduction of the price (unaware seller); compensation of all losses, including the dead animals or the building (knowing seller). Legal basis: the defect upsets the equivalence of goods and price; knowing concealment breaches BONA FIDES.
6. **Remedies**: ACTIO EMPTI (B v A), a BONAE FIDEI IUDICIUM. If the animal was a IUMENTUM or PECUS bought at the market, the aedilician actions may also come into question (p. 161). Timber is outside the edict.

### DOGMATIC EXPLANATION
7. **Similar cases**: Marcian D 18.1.45 (second-hand clothing sold as new: unaware seller liable for the value, aware seller also for the buyer's loss); D 19.1.13.1 (FUGITIVUS v FUR); Pomponius D 19.1.6.4 (vessels: liable even without knowledge because of an assurance); Examples 59–60 (timber, bunk bed and desk).
8. **Controversies**: none in the text; contrast Pomponius D 19.1.6.4, where a DOLUS view and Labeo's view are reported.
9. **Dogmatic**: distinguish loss caused by the defect (the timber is worth less) from consequential loss (the building, the other animals). Warranty in the strict sense only restores equivalence: price reduction or rescission, regardless of fault. Consequential loss is fault-based: it is owed only where the seller breached BONA FIDES, above all by concealing a defect he knew of (DOLUS, Florentinus D 18.1.43.2). This protects the honest seller from unforeseeable liability and makes the dishonest seller bear the full damage.

cards.q: D 19.1.13 pr: rotten timber; the building collapses. The seller did not know. What does the buyer get?
cards.a:
Only what he would have paid less had he known of the defect (price reduction), with the ACTIO EMPTI.
• No compensation for the building: that is consequential loss

cards.q: D 19.1.13 pr: a sick animal infects the buyer's herd; the seller knew. What does the buyer get?
cards.a:
All losses resulting from the purchase: his interest in having bought a healthy animal, incl. the infected animals.
• Basis: knowing concealment breaches BONA FIDES (ACTIO EMPTI)

9.title: Mini exegesis 3: D 21.1.31.11 (Ulpian; MORTUUS REDHIBETUR), Case 128
9.text:
Facts and decision as summarised in RLO pp. 163–164.

### BASIC PART
1. **Facts**: A sells and delivers a slave to B. The slave has a defect that A did not disclose. The slave dies before B can return him.
2. **Legal question**: Can B still set the sale aside although he can no longer return the slave? Must he compensate A for the slave?
3. **Decision**: ULPIAN. One must establish whether the slave died through the fault of B, his servants or his procurator. If so, the slave is treated as still alive, and B can redhibit only if he compensates A for the slave's value. If the slave died from a cause B is not answerable for, B may rescind without compensation.

### INTERPRETATIVE PART
4. **Institution**: aedilician warranty for quality defects in a market sale of slaves. The edict required the seller to declare MORBUS and VITIA; an undisclosed defect makes him liable whether or not he knew of it (pp. 161–162).
5. **Claims**: B v A: return of the price and reimbursement of his costs, against handing over all benefits drawn from the slave. A v B: compensation for the slave's value, if B is at fault for the death.
6. **Remedies**: ACTIO REDHIBITORIA (within six months): rescission EX TUNC with mutual restitution. Alternative: ACTIO QUANTI MINORIS (within twelve months), price reduction. Outside the edict: ACTIO EMPTI.

### DOGMATIC EXPLANATION
7. **Similar cases**: Exercise 41 (slave Peitho with a heart condition dies before being returned, RLO p. 174); D 21.1.58 pr and D 21.1.23.8 (runaway slave who takes the buyer's property: consequential loss in REDHIBITIO, or NOXAE DEDITIO).
8. **Controversies**: none in the text. The book notes that the rule fits best where the slave dies of the very illness that grounded redhibition; whether Ulpian meant only that case is unclear (p. 164).
9. **Dogmatic**: return of the goods is in principle a requirement of redhibition, because rescission aims to put the buyer where he would be had he never contracted. Strictly applied, the slave's death would end the remedy. Ulpian instead allocates the risk: the buyer bears the loss he is answerable for; the **seller bears the risk of accidental death**. Contrast the general rule PERICULUM EST EMPTORIS: here the undisclosed defect shifts the risk back to the seller. The legal proverb (PAROEMIA) is **MORTUUS REDHIBETUR**: the dead slave can be the object of redhibition.

terms.def: Legal proverb from Ulpian D 21.1.31.11: a dead slave can still be redhibited if the buyer is not answerable for the death (RLO p. 164).

cards.q: What does MORTUUS REDHIBETUR mean?
cards.a:
The dead slave can still be the object of redhibition (Ulpian D 21.1.31.11, Case 128).
• If the buyer is not answerable for the death, he rescinds without compensation
• The seller bears the risk of accidental death

cards.q: D 21.1.31.11: the defective slave dies through the buyer's fault before return. Can the buyer redhibit?
cards.a:
Yes, but the slave is treated as still alive: the buyer must compensate the seller for the slave's lost value.
• Fault of the buyer, his servants or his procurator counts

cards.q: Why is return of the goods normally a requirement of the ACTIO REDHIBITORIA?
cards.a: Because rescission puts the buyer where he would be had he never contracted: goods and price are returned (RLO p. 163).

10.title: Exegesis checklist: a fragment on warranty
10.text:
Work through this list when the exam text is about warranty. It follows the three-part structure from the method lesson (BASIC, INTERPRETATIVE, DOGMATIC).

| Step | Question to ask yourself |
|---|---|
| Sale | Is there an EMPTIO VENDITIO (agreement on goods and price)? Was the thing delivered by TRADITIO or by MANCIPATIO? RES MANCIPI? |
| Author | Who writes (INSCRIPTIO), whom does he cite, and whose opinion is the decision (e.g. Ulpian citing Julian)? |
| Defect type | Title (a third party claims IN REM) or quality (the thing itself is faulty)? |
| Timing | Did the defect or its cause exist at delivery? Arose after perfection by accident → PERICULUM EST EMPTORIS; by the seller's fault → non-performance; after delivery → nothing. |
| Title: property backdrop | Why did the buyer not become owner (NEMO PLUS IURIS)? Could USUCAPIO run (LEX ATINIA, BONA FIDES, one or two years)? |
| Title: eviction | Did a third party win with REI VINDICATIO, ACTIO PUBLICIANA or VINDICATIO PIGNORIS? Surrender, condemnation, or lost own suit? Chain of sales? |
| Title: remedy | Mancipation → ACTIO AUCTORITATIS (was the seller called in?); STIPULATIO DUPLAE → CONDICTIO; otherwise ACTIO EMPTI. Exceptions: knowing seller, stipulated ownership, EX ALIA CAUSA. |
| Quality: is it a defect? | Ordinary or agreed use impaired? DICTA ET PROMISSA? ID QUOD ACTUM EST? Apparent defect (CAVEAT EMPTOR) or mere sales talk? |
| Quality: edict? | Market sale of a slave, IUMENTUM or PECUS? MORBUS or listed VITIUM? → ACTIO REDHIBITORIA (6 months) / QUANTI MINORIS (12 months); MORTUUS REDHIBETUR. |
| Quality: ACTIO EMPTI | Seller unaware → reduction or rescission only. Seller knew (DOLUS) or gave an assurance → full interest incl. consequential loss. |
| Loss | Loss caused by the defect or consequential loss? Name the figure if the text gives one. |
| Agreement | Exclusion clause (invalid against DOLUS MALUS)? Quality stipulation (ID QUOD INTEREST)? |
| Similar cases | D 19.1.13 pr / .1, D 18.1.45, D 19.1.6.4, D 21.1.31.11, D 21.2.8, D 21.2.29 pr, D 21.2.16.1. |
| Controversies | D 19.1.6.4 (DOLUS view v Labeo); D 19.1.21.2 (missing NON?). Otherwise: 'none in the text'. |
| Dogmatic | Warranty restores equivalence regardless of fault; damages beyond that rest on BONA FIDES (fault) or a guarantee; eviction principle because USUCAPIO may cure the defect. |

### Three typical mistakes
1. Making the **third party** the defendant of the warranty claim. He sues the buyer IN REM; the buyer sues his own seller.
2. Giving the evicted buyer a claim **before eviction** without naming one of the three exceptions.
3. Awarding **consequential loss** against an unaware seller who gave no assurance.

cards.q: Exegesis of a warranty fragment: which question do you ask first after identifying the sale?
cards.a:
Is it a defect of title or of quality, and did it exist (at least its cause) at delivery?
• Later accident after perfection → risk; seller's fault before delivery → non-performance

cards.q: Three typical mistakes in a warranty exegesis?
cards.a:
1) Making the evicting third party the defendant of the warranty claim.
• 2) A title claim before eviction without naming an exception
• 3) Consequential loss against an unaware seller without an assurance
